analysis.one_liner: Turns federal school funding into private-school vouchers and repeals school meal nutrition standards.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on January 23, 2017 and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the nation's main federal K-12 education law and replace federal funding with block grants that states must pass out as vouchers—payments parents could use at private schools or for homeschooling. It would also repeal the 2012 rule requiring healthier school lunches and breakfasts—more fruits, vegetables, and whole grains, and less salt and fat. Only three Republican cosponsors joined the sponsor, and the bill never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Families who already use or would use private schools and homeschooling would receive federal payments toward tuition and costs. Private schools gain a stream of public tuition dollars without new obligations, and school food-service suppliers no longer face the 2012 nutrition standards.

how_it_helps.text: Parents who enroll a child in a private school or homeschool would receive a federal payment covering costs like tuition, fees, and transportation, capped at those costs.

Federal oversight of K-12 education would be sharply reduced: the Elementary and Secondary Education Act would be repealed and the Education Department limited to approving state applications and sending block grants.
Schools would no longer have to meet the 2012 nutrition standards requiring more fruits, vegetables, and whole grains and less sodium and saturated fat in meals.

analysis.who_pays: Public schools would lose federal dollars when students take vouchers elsewhere, and the repeal of the ESEA would end the federal programs—including targeted aid for low-income students—that the law funds. Children in school meal programs would lose the nutritional guarantees of the repealed rule.

drawbacks.text: Voucher amounts would be divided equally among all eligible children in a state, so districts serving low-income students would no longer receive the additional federal weight they get under current law.

Repealing the 2012 nutrition rule would remove requirements that school meals include more fruits, vegetables, and whole grains and less sodium and saturated fat, affecting meal quality for the tens of millions of children in the national lunch and breakfast programs.
Vouchers would not cover the full cost of most private school tuition, so families who could not make up the difference would effectively be excluded.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would shift federal education money toward families already choosing private options and away from the targeted aid that follows low-income students, while removing nutritional standards for school meals. Whether the voucher amount would be enough to open private schooling to families who cannot already afford it is not addressed in the bill's funding structure, which divides money evenly per child with no low-income weighting.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on January 23, 2017 and sat there for the rest of the Congress with no hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Steve King (R-IA) with three Republican cosponsors on January 23, 2017.
It was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day and received no further action through the end of the 115th Congress.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote on the bill appears in its action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public school systems and the federal school lunch and breakfast programs are unaffected, since the bill never advanced. Families hoping to use federal vouchers for private school or homeschooling gained nothing from its failure to advance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Public schools and school meal programs

for.name: Reps. Andy Harris and Trent Franks

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 23, 2017 and took no further action on it for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats were involved, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: Vouchers would create a new stream of federal tuition dollars for private schools with no added obligations attached. The cost would fall on public school budgets as students and their per-pupil funding left.
Federal funds would follow students out of public schools to private options, and the repeal of the ESEA would end existing federal K-12 programs, including aid targeted to low-income students.

Repealing the 2012 nutrition rule would lift requirements for more fruits, vegetables, and whole grains and less sodium and fat in meals, reducing constraints on school meal programs and their suppliers.
